title: How to Run an AI Pilot at a Personal Injury Firm: A 30-Day Scorecard
summary: Plan a 30-day AI agent pilot at your personal injury firm: pick one job, write the playbook, train case managers, and measure what matters.
body_markdown:
Most personal injury firms have tried AI by now. Far fewer have let an AI agent work real cases alongside their team. That gap is where a pilot either earns trust or quietly dies.


The numbers show the gap. The 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report found 69% of legal professionals personally use generative AI at work, up from 31% a year earlier. A 2026 Thomson Reuters Institute report found 15% of professional services organizations have adopted any agentic AI tool, and only 18% track return on their AI spend (both[as cited in Courting the Law](https://courtingthelaw.com/2026/11/20/commentary/legal-ai-has-moved-past-the-chatbot-most-lawyers-havent) , Nov. 20, 2026). Firms are using chat tools. Few are measuring agents. And as[Above the Law](https://abovethelaw.com/2026/11/law-firms-need-an-ai-strategy-not-another-ai-subscription/) put it this month, many firms add AI one subscription at a time while policy and training lag behind.


A good pilot fixes that. Here is a 30-day plan for a managing partner or operations lead who wants a clear yes or no at the end.


## 1. Give the agent one job


Don't turn on everything for every case. Pick one task your team does constantly and resents doing, like confirming a client made their appointment or chasing a provider for records. A narrow pilot gives you a clean read. A big-bang launch gives you noise.


The same goes for each client. A client only has so much attention. If an agent asks for check-ins, documents and reminders all in the same week, replies drop across the board, including on the messages that matter.


## 2. Pick a small team and new cases


Two case managers and a legal assistant is plenty. Start on new cases so clients meet the agent from the beginning instead of mid-case. Pick people who will tell you the truth, including the skeptic.


## 3. Write the playbook before day one


An agent is only as good as what your firm tells it. Before launch, write down:


- **Your FAQs by phase.** What clients usually ask during treatment, while the demand is out, and in negotiation. Thin FAQs produce an agent that escalates everything.
- **Your introduction.** Who is texting, on whose behalf, and that it is AI. Clients who understand who is reaching out reply far more often than clients who get a cold task message.
- **Your escalation rules.** Exactly when a person takes over: a request for a human, frustration, new pain or symptoms, a missed appointment with no response.


## 4. Train the case managers too


This is where most pilots break. When an agent starts answering routine texts, case managers stop seeing every inbound message. If nobody shows them what an escalation looks like and where to find it, a client can wait for days. Walk each person on the pilot team through a real escalation before go-live.


## 5. Set the scorecard before you start


Write down your baseline in week zero, then measure the same things at day 30.


- **Handled without escalation.** The share of client messages the agent resolved on its own.
- **Escalation response time.** How long a flagged client waited for a person.
- **The outcome you picked in step 1.** Appointments confirmed, records received, gaps in care caught.
- **Client reaction.** Reply rates, opt-outs and complaints.
- **Team time.** A simple weekly estimate from each case manager of hours spent on the task.
- **Errors.** Anything the agent said that a case manager would have said differently.


## 6. Watch closely, then less closely


Review conversations daily in week one and weekly after that. Close attention in the first month is healthy. It is how your team learns where the agent is strong and where your playbook needs another line.


## 7. Decide what "pass" means now


Agree on the bar before you see results. For example: errors are rare and caught by review, escalations get a human reply the same day, and the pilot team says they want to keep it. Set the end date and put the decision meeting on the calendar.


## How a pilot with Lia works


Lia, your case liaison, is built to start small. Firms usually turn on one skill first, often appointment follow-up, and expand once the team trusts it. Your firm writes the FAQs and escalation rules in plain language. Every escalation carries the reason and what Lia already tried. Lia's default introduction says it is AI, and the copy is editable. Lia gives no legal or medical advice and only starts conversations between 9am and 7pm in the firm's local time. A team dashboard shows escalations, drafts and time saved, and a Clients to Review list shows who needs a person.


One early result: Voto & Cavalli, P.C. reported a 78.8% appointment attendance rate across 166 appointments tracked on Lia between its May 2026 go-live and mid-June. Hear how their case manager runs it in our[Hona Huddle recap](https://www.hona.com/post/hona-huddle-why-pi-clients-stop-treating) , or read[Meet Lia](https://www.hona.com/post/meet-lia-ai-case-agent) .


## FAQ


### How long should an AI pilot last at a law firm?


Thirty days is enough for one focused task. It gives you a few weeks of real conversations after the setup week, which is long enough to judge accuracy and team adoption.


### What should a personal injury firm measure in an AI pilot?


The share of messages handled without escalation, how fast escalated clients hear from a person, the outcome the agent was assigned (like appointments kept or records received), client reaction, staff time and errors.


### Should clients know they are texting with AI?


Yes. Clients engage more when the first message explains who is texting and why, and several state bars now point toward disclosure. Check your state's guidance.


### Who should be on the pilot team?


A small group, usually two case managers and a legal assistant, working new cases. Include at least one skeptic so the feedback is honest.
